             RESPONSE OF INTERVENORS THE MOSELEY GROUP
          AND THE V8 LANDOWNERS COALITION TO THE EXCEPTIONS
                        OF CERTAIN INTERVENORS

       Intervenors James Gregory Waller, Marilyn Moseley Waller, Arthur Kyle Moseley, David

Moseley (Moseley Group) and the V8 Landowners Coalition submit this Response to the

Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (PFD) filed by certain intervenors. The Moseley Group

and the V8 Landowners Coalition will at times be called the “Multiple Intervenors.”

       Specifically, Multiple Intervenors file this Response to the Exceptions to the PFD filed by

Solana Intervenors, The Brady Creek Intervenors, Staten Creek Ranch, and 4K Land & Cattle.

Multiple Intervenors do not necessarily agree with other intervenors, and their failure to

specifically identify an intervenor should not be construed as agreeing with their Exceptions.

       As required by the Exceptions and Replies memorandum, this Response will follow the

outline of the PFD. Multiple Intervenors’ Response is limited to Issues 8-10, Routing Criteria.




                                                1
     URISDICTION, PROCEDURAL HISTORY, APPLICABLE LAW, PRELIMINARY
           ORDER ISSUES (1-4), DUE PROCESS, AND NEED (ISSUES 5-7)


         Multiple Intervenors take no position on these matters and have no exceptions.


                                ISSUE NOS. 8-10; ROUTE SELECTION

         Route 894 best meets PUC criteria. The Exceptions of these certain intervenors fail to

demonstrate that Route 392, or any other route, is better supported by the evidence. Multiple

Intervenors will not identify every deficiency in their Exceptions but will discuss some that are

relevant to route selection.

                                     Solana and Brady Creek Intervenors

         For example, Solana Intervenors erroneously claim that PUC Staff witness John Poole

recommended “a northern crossing that uses existing transmission infrastructure.1” As support for

this statement, Solana Intervenors cite their own Initial Brief at 92. Page 9 of its Initial Brief makes

the same statement but cites no evidentiary support for it3. In fact, Mr. Poole recommended Route

487, which Solana Intervenors acknowledge is in the Central Corridor4.

         On the very next page of their Exceptions, Solana Intervenors state that Link U3 “is the

only link that uses existing transmission infrastructure5. Mr. Poole did not recommend a route that

included U3, further contradicting Solana Intervenors’ claim that Mr. Poole recommended a

crossing that uses existing transmission infrastructure.

         Mr. Poole was aware that Route 392 uses Link U3 to cross the Colorado River and that this

crossing has an existing transmission line. Rather than recommending Route 392, Mr. Poole (and

 others) acknowledged that crossing a river next to another transmission line increases the risks of

simultaneous outages6.

        Others among these certain intervenors cite how Mr. Poole acknowledged the benefits

following existing infrastructure; they fail to mention that Mr. Poole also sees risks of having two

transmission lines crossing the Colorado River at the same location7.

        The Exceptions of the Brady Creek Intervenors (authored by the same lawyer) also extol

link U3’s virtues but the analysis of environmental concerns is similarly limited. Route 894’s Link

J22 will cross in a perpendicular manner and will not run parallel to the Colorado River8. In sharp

contrast, U3’s crossing is not perpendicular; U3 runs parallel to the Colorado River for almost two

miles9. The PFD specifically noted the value of Route 894 not running parallel to any streams10.

        U3 crosses at an ecologically significant stream segment (ESSS)11; Link J22 does not12.

U3 crosses at USFWS critical habitat13; J22 does not14. Only U3 crosses within the North-Central

Prairies major land resource area (MLRA)15, where most of the rainfall occurs during high-

intensity convective thunderstorms16. U3’s proximity to an existing transmission line in an area of

high-intensity convective thunderstorms elevates the risk of simultaneous outages17. Finally, U3

crosses an area with multiple river bends18; J22 does not19.

            The Solana Intervenors, the Brady Creek Intervenors, and their experts suggest that Route

392’s crossing of the Colorado River is so positive and the value of Route 894’s attributes is so

minimal that little or no weight should be given to any consideration other than the Colorado River

Crossing. The ALJ’s were correct in rejecting this suggestion in preparing the PFD; they should

continue to reject it.

                                                 Staten Creek Ranch

           The Exceptions of Staten Creek Ranch discuss Dr. Sansom’s testimony about the

importance of the Colorado Crossing. This is the same Dr. Sansom who admitted he did not realize

that Link U3 was in the North-Central Prairies major land resource area (MLRA)20, where most of

the rainfall occurs during high-intensity convective thunderstorms21. As such, he did not account

for the risk of simultaneous outages, and the increased risk of more severe grid disruption, due to

U3 being in proximity to another transmission line in an MLRA known for high-intensity

convective thunderstorms.

           Indeed, none of the experts for these certain intervenors addressed the increased risks of

major grid disruption presented by two transmission lines in close proximity crossing a large river

in an MLRA known for high-intensity convective thunderstorms.

           Moreover, these experts largely ignored the environmental concerns raised by Link U3,

due to it paralleling the Colorado River for almost two miles, not using a perpendicular crossing,

crossing at an ESSS, and crossing at a USFWS critical habitat. By minimizing the risks of

paralleling a transmission line and ignoring other environmental concerns, these experts failed to

reach the correct conclusion: the environmental and aesthetic value of Link U3 is at best marginal.




20
     Id. at 3-6 (Figure 3-2B) and Figure 6-L Panel 4
21
     Id. at 3-3

                                                         4
                                             4K Land & Cattle

        Dr. Turnbough’s work is discussed in the Exceptions of 4K Land & Cattle. Dr. Turnbough

characterized the difference in habitable structures between Route 392 and Route 894 (a difference

of 51 structures over 225 miles) as numerically insignificant22. Just three weeks before, he called

a difference of 105 structures over 365 miles (140 miles longer) a “large disparity23.” When asked

about how he can characterize one as “numerically insignificant” and another as “large disparity,”

he admitted: “There is no standard24.” An expert who expresses opinions in the absence of a

standard, in essence giving a “because I say so” opinion, is of no assistance to a fact finder.

        4K Ranch also fails to understand the “prudent avoidance” policy. The policy does not give

significant weight to 4K Ranch’s concern that it may need to relocate activities within or incur

increased operating costs for its “actively managed, regularly inhabited 100,000-acre ranch”25.

4K’s Exceptions suggest that some relocation or management effort to have a transmission line

within a 100,000-acre ranch is a greater “prudent avoidance” issue than locating the line close to

an elementary school with 530 students26. As support, 4K cites to Mr. King’s testimony, where

he discusses but does not quantify changes his ranch may need to take as a result of the

transmission line.

         Of course, Texas law is clear that if land acquired by eminent domain renders a structure

that remains in an unsafe location, the landowner can recover the cost of moving the structure.27

Also, to the extent 4K Ranch is able to reasonably estimate increased operating costs, Texas law

driveways or other improvements may be compensable.” That principle was followed in State v. Stockton Bend 100
Joint Venture, 2016 WL 3198960, at 10 (Tex. App.-Ft. Worth, 2016, review denied), where recovery of costs to
remedy access rendered unsafe by the taking were affirmed.

 allows it to be compensated for increased operating costs caused by a taking28.

         Prudent avoidance has its limits. The policy is not designed to minimize inconvenience to

owners of 100,000-acre ranches.

   OTHER PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES (ISSUES 11-16), UNCONTESTED
MATTERS, SUMMARY, FINDINGS OF FACT, CONCLUSIONS OF LAW, PROPOSED
                     ORDERING PARAGRAPHS


         Multiple Intervenors agree with and support Findings 156-250. As to other Findings,

Multiple Intervenors take no position and have no exceptions.

                                                 CONCLUSION

         Multiple Intervenors urge the ALJs to make no substantive changes to the PFD based on

the Exceptions of these certain intervenors.

         The Exceptions Letter can and should state, “Route 392 utilizes a Colorado River crossing

with a pre-existing infrastructure corridor; however, the specific infrastructure is an existing

transmission line. This proximity would increase the risk of simultaneous outages and more severe

electric grid disruptions. Regarding other environmental considerations, Route 894’s Colorado

River crossing (Link J22) is superior to Route 392’s crossing.”

         The ALJs may issue an Exceptions Letter in response to Exceptions filed by the Applicants

or the PUC Staff, or in response to recent PUC decisions and guidance. Regardless of other

possible changes, the PFD was correct that if a route should be selected, Route 894 best complies

with PUC criteria. That conclusion and the proposed Findings related to it should not change.



28
  Texas Power & Light Co. v. Trinity Valley Ranch Co., 395 S.W.2d 866, 870-871 (1965), “The growing crops must
be sprayed by airplane with an insecticide, and the towers and wires erected and to be erected by appellant greatly
impede the spraying on and near the easement with the result that insects tend to spread to other portions of the ranch.
Seeds of weeds are spread by birds resting on the cables and are blown to other parts of the Ranch. Plowing and
cultivation are rendered difficult and inconvenient...These and other matters were testified to by witnesses in support
of their testimony that the taking of the easement would damage the remainder of the property, especially the 3439-
acre tract. These elements are properly to be considered in assessing values and damages.”
